cards.md:
# Building a sea island

This tutorial builds a large island in an open sea: a grassy hill with a lower one beside it, a wall of cliffs on the north east coast, a sandy beach on the south shore and dirt paths winding from the beach up to the hilltops. Then it plants the island with a woodland, bushes, boulders and meadow grass that all keep clear of the paths, and adds a small jetty with a few props. It uses one terrain, a handful of brushes and the Sculpt, Blend and Scatter tools. The island is about 380 m across, big enough to walk around for a while.

cards.alt: The finished island seen from the south: beach, jetty, paths, woodland and cliffs

cards.md: The numbers below are the ones used for the pictures, in the demo project's units (32 per meter). They are a starting point, not a recipe; the terrain generator gives every seed a different coastline. If you have not read it yet, [[terrain-painting]] explains what the brushes do underneath, which makes the choices here easier to follow.

## Choose the four layers

A terrain can blend four textures, so decide first which four the island needs. This one uses the demo textures in `showcase/`:

| Layer | Material | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `showcase/grass` | everything that is not something else |
| 1 | `showcase/cliff` | steep ground and cliff faces |
| 2 | `showcase/dirt` | the paths |
| 3 | `showcase/sand` | the shore and the beach |

Grass goes in layer 0 because it is the default ground: a fresh terrain is all layer 0, and erasing paints it back. The order of the others does not matter, but the Create Terrain dialog names its four slots after what *Auto Paint* would put there (base, slope, peak, low), so following that order keeps the dialog honest.

## Create the terrain

1. Open *Terrain > Create Terrain...*.
2. Set **Resolution** to 257 x 257 and leave **Cell size** at 64. The dialog shows the size, 16384 units or 512 m on a side.
3. Pick the **Island** shape, set **Height** to 1600 and **Feature size** to 3000. Larger features give a calmer coastline with fewer tiny bays. Keep the default octaves, roughness and erosion.
4. Type the four materials into the layer rows: `showcase/grass`, `showcase/cliff`, `showcase/dirt` and `showcase/sand`, with a tile of 256 for the first two and 192 for the others.
5. Untick **3D cursor** next to **Center** and set the center to `0 -576 0`.
6. Untick **Paint layers from slope and height** and press **Create**.

cards.alt: The Create Terrain dialog with the island settings

cards.md:
The island shape rises from the edges to the middle, and the center's height is where the terrain's zero sits. The sea will be at height 0, so the terrain goes 576 units below it: only its middle stays dry, and a wide ring of shallow sea floor is left around the coast. If you forget, the terrain's **Origin** in the Inspector moves it afterwards; the origin is the corner, so there it reads `-8192 -576 -8192`.

Auto paint is off because this tutorial paints by hand, which takes a few minutes and gives far better control. If you want a quick first pass instead, tick **Bands from sea level** under the auto paint box and leave it at 0. Without it the bands are measured from the lowest point of the terrain, and on an island that is the sea floor, so the low band would sit under water.

## Add the sea

The sea is a single flat brush. Draw a box in the Top view that reaches far past the terrain on every side, then use the Front view to make it 32 units thick with its top face at height 0. Give it `showcase/water` from the Materials panel and set the scale in the Inspector's *Alignment* section to 8 by 8 so the ripples are not tiny. Finally right click it and choose *Create Brush Entity > func_illusionary*: an illusionary brush is drawn but has no collision, so the player can wade in instead of walking on the water.

Make the box generous, several times the size of the terrain. Its far edge is otherwise visible on the horizon from the hilltops.

cards.alt: The generated island sitting in the sea, before any sculpting

cards.md:
## Raise the hills

The generated island is fairly flat, so the next step is to give it a shape you can recognise from the beach. Press **G** for the Sculpt tool and set the mode to **Raise**. Nothing needs to be selected: with an empty selection the tool works on every terrain in the map.

1. Set the **radius** to 2800 and keep the strength around 4. Hold the button over a spot a little west of the centre until the hill stands about 1500 units, 47 m, above the sea. The ring shows the brush, and the status bar shows the position under the cursor, height included.
2. Drop the radius to about 1300 and press a few times on the same spot to give the hill a steeper top.
3. Raise a second, lower hill to the south east with a radius of about 1900.

cards.alt: The Sculpt tool in Raise mode with a 2800 unit brush over the main hill

cards.md: A huge brush and a low strength is the way to work at this scale. Small brushes make lumps, and lumps are what give a terrain away as hand made. If something goes too far, hold **Ctrl** while dragging to smooth it back.

## Build the cliffs

Cliffs need a lot of height over a short distance, more than a smooth brush will ever make. Three passes get there:

1. With **Raise** and a radius of about 1800, drag along the north east coast, a little inland, to lift a broad headland that leans against the main hill. Then give the whole island one pass of **Smooth** with a very large brush, so the headland and the hills blend into each other.
2. Switch to **Lower** with a radius of about 1000 and drag along the sea just in front of that coast. Deeper water right at the foot of the headland makes the drop steeper.
3. Switch to **Terrace**, set **step** to 300 and the radius to 1000, and drag along the coastline. Terrace pulls heights towards whole multiples of the step, so the slope breaks into flat shelves and steep faces. A step of 300 units, about 9 m, gives two or three tiers on this headland. Finish with a light **Smooth** along the same line to take the sharpest edges off.

cards.alt: The Sculpt tool in Terrace mode with a 300 unit step along the north east coast

cards.md: The faces are still grass at this point. They turn into rock once the painting starts, which is the reason to sculpt everything first: paint stays where it was put, and a cliff raised after painting keeps the grass it had.

## Shape the beach

A beach is a flat strip just above the water. Switch the Sculpt tool to **Flatten**, which pulls the ground towards the height where the stroke started. Set a radius of about 900, start the stroke right at the waterline on the south shore and drag along the coast. Everything under the brush settles to that height, a few units above the sea. Finish with **Smooth** and a slightly larger brush so the beach runs into the land behind it without a step.

cards.alt: The Sculpt tool in Flatten mode on the south shore

cards.md:
## Paint the sand

Now switch to the Blend tool with **Shift+G**. The shore is the first thing to paint, and the height mask does it for the whole island at once.

1. Set the mode to **height**, the falloff to **constant**, the layer to **3** and the strength to 1.
2. Set the height range from `-3000` to `40`. Everything below 40 units, a little over a meter above the sea, is shore.
3. Set the radius to 12000, big enough to cover the whole island, and click once in the middle.

cards.alt: The Blend tool in height mode: one click paints sand on everything below 40 units

cards.md: Every coast now has a band of sand that fades into the grass over a couple of meters, and the flattened beach in the south is almost all sand. To widen the beach further, switch to **paint** with a smooth falloff, radius 700 and a strength around 0.7, and drag along the south shore once.

## Paint the rock

Rock goes on the cliffs the same way, with the slope mask instead of the height mask.

1. Set the mode to **slope**, keep the falloff **constant**, set the layer to **1** and the range to `32` to `90` degrees.
2. With the same huge radius, click once over the island.

cards.alt: The Blend tool in slope mode: everything steeper than 32 degrees turns to rock

cards.md: The terraced faces of the cliffs turn to rock and their shelves stay green, which is exactly what makes them read as cliffs. Steep patches on the hills and the bank behind the beach get small outcrops of rock as well. If one of them sits where you do not want it, paint over it with layer 0 or use **erase**.

## Paint the paths

Paths are the part that follows no rule, so they are painted by hand with the plain **paint** mode.

1. Set the mode to **paint**, the falloff to **smooth**, the layer to **2**, the radius to 140 and the strength to 0.8.
2. Start at the top of the beach and drag up towards the main hill in long, gentle curves. On the steep upper slope, zigzag instead of going straight up; that is how a real path climbs and it reads that way from a distance.
3. Paint a second path from the top of the main hill along the ridge to the cliff top, and a third from the east end of the beach to the second hill.

cards.alt: The Blend tool in paint mode with a 140 unit brush on the path up the main hill

cards.md:
The radius matters more than it seems. The paint is stored on the terrain's vertices, 64 units apart here, and a brush narrower than about two cells comes out ragged or broken up. A radius of 140 gives a path about 7 m wide with clean edges. For a narrow footpath, lay a mesh or a decal on top instead. [[terrain-painting]] shows what different widths look like.

Strokes can be repainted as often as you like. Dragging over the edge of a path with **smooth** softens it, and a few dabs of grass (layer 0) with a spray falloff make the border look trodden rather than drawn.

cards.alt: The path climbing the main hill, seen from the slope below

cards.md:
## Break up the repeat

From high up, the rock shows a regular pattern where the same texture repeats every 256 units. The layers' **detile** setting hides it. Select the terrain and, in the Inspector, set detile to 0.5 on grass and dirt, 0.4 on sand and 0.7 with a sharpen of 0.4 on the cliff layer. The difference is easiest to see on the cliffs, compared in [[terrain-painting]].

cards.alt: The terrain's layers in the Inspector with detile set on every layer

cards.md:
## Plant the woodland

Trees, bushes and grass come from the **Scatter** tool. Press **B** and the Scatter panel opens next to the Inspector. Everything you scatter lives in a scatter set on its own layer, and each set is its own palette: its models are the cards in the panel, each with a weight and a switch that decides whether the brush paints it.

1. Press **Preset** and pick *mixed woodland*. It starts a set with twelve broadleaf trees. **Rename** it to `woodland`.
2. A set only lands on its targets. Click the eyedropper next to **Targets** and then the terrain, so it shows under Targets.
3. In the **Brush** section set **Density** to 0.16, **Slope** from 0 to 30 degrees, tick **Height** and set it from 120 to 2000, and give **Seed** any number.
4. Press **Fill targets**.

The height range keeps the trees above the sand, the slope range keeps them off the cliffs, and the density is instances per 64 by 64 units, so 0.16 is roughly one tree every 5 m where nothing else is in the way. Every model's spacing keeps trees from growing into each other.

cards.alt: The woodland set in the Scatter panel after Fill targets

cards.md: Fill covers the paths too, so clear them next. Switch the panel to **Erase** (or hold Shift), set the **Radius** to 260 and drag along each path. Erase only removes from the active set, whatever else grows there. Two short clicks with a larger brush open a clearing on the main hilltop and a meadow behind the beach.

cards.alt: Erasing the woodland off the path with a 260 unit brush

cards.md:
## Hero trees and bushes

A second set with the *detailed forest* preset holds a few hero trees, with three to four times the detail of the woodland, for the places a player looks at up close. Paint them with single clicks where the paths leave the beach and around the hilltop clearing: radius 260, density 0.08, slope 0 to 30 and Height unticked. Clicking is enough, a stroke would plant far more than a handful.

cards.alt: Hero trees painted with single clicks at the foot of the path

cards.md:
Bushes mark the edge of the wood. Start a set from the *bushes* preset, target the terrain and fill it with density 0.35, slope 0 to 32 and Height from 45 to 200. That is a band just above the sand, so the bushes line the top of the beach and thin out under the trees. Erase them off the paths with a radius of 190.

Leave **Keep spacing to other sets** ticked for all of them. With it, a new set keeps its models' spacing from what the other sets placed, so no bush grows through a trunk.

cards.alt: Bushes filled into a height band just above the sand

cards.md:
## Boulders on the cliffs

Start a set from the *boulders* preset and target the terrain. This time paint instead of filling: set the radius to 1100, density 0.035, slope 12 to 50 and Height from 20 upwards, then drag once along the top of the north east cliffs. The slope range puts the boulders on the ledges and the steep grass above the rock, and the height keeps them out of the water.

cards.alt: Boulders painted along the cliffs in one stroke

cards.md:
## Grass, and grass on the boulders

The *grass* preset is a foliage set: grass, tall grass, flowers and ferns, without collision or shadows, fading out with distance. Start one, target the terrain and paint the meadows and clearings with a big brush: radius 650, density 2.5, slope 0 to 28 and Height from 45. Foliage is dense and small, so keep it to the open ground a player walks through rather than filling the whole island. Erase it off the paths with a radius of 170.

cards.alt: Meadow grass painted into the clearing behind the beach

cards.md: A scatter set can be another set's target. Start one more grass set, click the eyedropper and then one of the boulders: the whole *cliff boulders* set becomes the target, and the terrain is not. **Fill targets** with density 6 and slope 0 to 45 now grows grass and flowers on the tops of the boulders only. The grass is placed on the boulders as they are when you fill, so finish the boulders first.

cards.alt: Grass growing on a boulder: the set's only target is the boulder set

cards.md:
## A jetty and a few props

The jetty is plain brushes on a layer of its own. Draw the deck from the top of the beach straight out to sea: 128 units wide, 1100 long and 8 thick, with its top 48 units above the water, in `showcase/planks`. Under it go two rows of 16 unit square posts in `showcase/beam`, every 200 units, reaching well below the sea floor so they never float. Two short posts at the far end make a railing.

The props come from the demo project's Poly Haven folder. *File > Import > Model Prop (.bbmodel, .glb)...* places a `prop_model` entity at the 3D cursor that Godot loads from its `res://` path. Two `wooden_crate_01` stacked at the end of the deck, a `wine_barrel_01`, a `lifebuoy` leaning on a post and an `ocean_buoy` out in the water are enough to make it look used.

cards.alt: The jetty from the sea, with crates, a barrel and the lifebuoy

cards.md:
## See it in Godot

Save the map inside your Godot project and build it with a `FuncGodotMap` node, as described in [[building-in-godot]]. The terrain arrives as a `GodotTrenchTerrain` with its chunks, collision and the same four layer blend, the sea brush as an illusionary mesh at height 0, and every scatter set as MultiMeshes with shared collision shapes. The foliage sets have no collision and fade out with distance, the trees and boulders collide.

cards.alt: The finished island built and rendered in Godot
The jetty in Godot

cards.md: The island is also recorded as an MCP script, `examples/mcp/sea_island.json` in the repository. Replaying it in a running editor rebuilds this exact island, terrain, scatter sets and jetty, step for step, which makes it a handy reference for the numbers used above.
